segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter Ames dried his grandmother's formulary on his shop counter, between two bowls of sand, with the shutters open to the afternoon. The tide-mark ran across the bottom third of every page. Jory Brennick spent a quarter of an hour on one smudged figure before he would say it aloud.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Fourth trial. Ground stone, one part in forty. Water boiled and stood till cold. Three spoons at the turn of each watch.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He looked up.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: One part in forty. That's a thumbnail in a bucket.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: That's why she burned the first three sets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter had the loupe to his eye and a strip of paper under the line, moving it down a word at a time.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: She writes that the second trial was stronger and did harm. She does not say how much. She was not writing for me.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: So you make it up in your back room and try it on somebody.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said it flatly, which was not how he said most things, and set the loupe down.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: I sell bay and camomile and a salve for chilblains. I have never weighed out a part in forty, and I'd be guessing at the grinding. There's a healer on Dunnock Lane with a balance and brass weights the size of peas. The book goes to her, and the stone with it, wrapped as it is.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: You've waited twenty years to hold that book.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: And my grandmother waited a winter to get the measures right. I'd not spoil her work in an afternoon to say I'd done it myself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They walked up to Dunnock Lane before the light went. The healer took the formulary in both hands and stood aside for them. Walter began to tell her where it came from.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: It was written by my grandmother. She kept the apothecary's shop on Kettle Row, down in the old town, and her family name was —

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stopped. He tried once more, and the word was not there to try with. Then he reached into his coat and unfolded the letter on the healer's own table, with the signature at the foot of it.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: There. That's her hand, and that's the name on it. I find I can't say it aloud any more. Read the second page before you decide what to make of that.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The healer read the second page standing up, and then sat down and read it again.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hammer frame went out over Kettle Row the next morning, an hour after the tide turned, on the day Selah Vance had said it would. Jory stood on the Shoreside walkway and watched the first piling drop into the water above the dyers' yard.

segments.speaker: Selah Vance
segments.text: Clear below?

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Clear. Nothing down there now but a post with four empty holes in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three days after that, a girl came down to Floatsome with a note for Jory. The healer had made up the draught to the fourth set of measures and tried it on two households off Cutler Street, where the fever had been worst. Both had kept their food down by the second morning. She wanted more of the stone, and she wanted it weighed by her and nobody else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter Ames paid him on the platform that evening, counted out full, and then pushed a second sum across the boards.

segments.speaker: Walter Ames
segments.text: That's for the woman who remembered a lantern that didn't move.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud looked at the coins for a while before she put her hand flat over them and drew them in.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: I'd have told you for nothing. I'll take it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora Quill sat on the edge of the boards with her heels in the water.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: She wants more stone.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Off the crack itself. Out past the dyers, where the floor opened.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: Then that's our next contract, and I'm not being called your partner on it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Co-signed. Both names on the paper.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud got up and went for her chart case.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Not until I've been over that ground with a line and drawn it properly. We went down Kettle Row on a chart four years out of date, and it nearly cost us the only door that shop had.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: And if the drawing takes a month?

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Then the fissure's been there twenty years and it'll keep a month. This time we map it first.
